Why not the others: (B) ignores transverse contraction. (C) converts area or strain with a factor-ten error. (D) reverses the net resistance change.
Key point: Specify the approximation order when coupling elastic and electrical changes.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Removal of one parallel heat-loss channel shifts the steady radiative temperature
questions.syllabus_anchor: Thermal Properties of Matter: heat transfer; radiation; thermal balance
questions.question: A body at steady temperature T0 receives 10 W and loses 6 W by conduction, with the remaining loss by thermal radiation to a fixed environment. The conductive link is removed, incident power remains 10 W and radiation increases monotonically with body temperature. Which statement follows?
options: A) Radiation was 6 W, and the new steady temperature is lower
B) Radiation was 4 W, and the temperature must remain T0
C) Radiation was 10 W, and no temperature adjustment is needed
D) Radiation was 4 W, and the new steady temperature is higher than T0
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Initial radiation is 4 W, and removal of conduction requires a higher steady temperature.
Given: Input power is constant and only the specified heat-loss channels operate.
Formula/Principle: At steady state total outward power equals inward power.
Step 1: \[P_{rad}(T_0)=10-6=4\ \mathrm W.\]
Step 2: Without conduction, at T0 only 4 W escapes while 10 W enters, so internal energy initially rises. New equilibrium requires radiation alone to reach 10 W.
Worked derivation: Since \(P_{rad}(T)\) is increasing, \(P_{rad}(T_{new})=10>4=P_{rad}(T_0)\) implies \(T_{new}>T_0\).
Why: Removing a heat-loss route does not remove the energy input; another route must carry more power at the new equilibrium.
Why not the others: (A) confuses the two original losses. (B) violates energy balance at the retained temperature. (C) ignores the original conductive power.
Key point: Evaluate the initial power imbalance before predicting the new thermal state.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Equal thermodynamic states need not have equal laboratory molecular energy when one gas drifts
questions.syllabus_anchor: Kinetic Theory: ideal-gas pressure; molecular energy; relative motion
questions.question: Two dilute packets of the same monatomic ideal gas have the same rest-frame pressure and number density. Packet A has zero mean laboratory velocity. Packet B has uniform laboratory drift speed U equal to its thermal rms speed w relative to its own mean motion. What is the ratio of mean molecular kinetic energy in the laboratory, B divided by A?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The laboratory mean kinetic-energy ratio is 2.
Given: Pressure and number density refer to random thermal motion in each packet's own rest frame.
Formula/Principle: p=nkT and the mean square of bulk plus zero-mean random velocity is U²+w².
Step 1: Equal p/n gives equal T and therefore equal thermal w² for the same gas. A has \(\langle v_A^2\rangle=w^2\).
Step 2: For B, the cross term vanishes because the random velocity has zero mean: \[\langle v_B^2\rangle=U^2+w^2=2w^2.\]
Worked derivation: \[\frac{\langle K_B\rangle}{\langle K_A\rangle}=\frac{m(2w^2)/2}{mw^2/2}=2.\]
Why: Thermal pressure fixes random-motion energy, not the additional energy of uniform bulk translation in a chosen laboratory frame.
Why not the others: (A) omits bulk kinetic energy. (C) reports a speed ratio instead of an energy ratio. (D) adds rms speeds as collinear deterministic velocities before squaring.
Key point: Separate thermal motion from the velocity of the gas as a whole.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: A delayed same-frequency contribution changes the resultant SHM amplitude through phase
questions.syllabus_anchor: Oscillations: simple harmonic motion; superposition
questions.question: Two measured displacements are added. The first is x1=A cos(ωt). At time τ=T/3, where T=2π/ω, a second independent oscillator begins contributing x2=A cos[ω(t-τ)]. For t≥τ, what is the amplitude of x1+x2? The addition is a superposition of two signals, not an impulsive change to either oscillator.
options: A) 2A
B) √3 A
C) A
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The resultant amplitude is A.
Given: Equal frequencies and amplitudes, with a start-time phase difference ωτ=2π/3.
Formula/Principle: Add same-frequency displacements as phasors or use the cosine sum identity.
Step 1: \[x_1+x_2=2A\cos(\omega\tau/2)\cos(\omega t-\omega\tau/2).\]
Step 2: Since \(\omega\tau/2=\pi/3\), the prefactor is \(2A(1/2)=A\).
Worked derivation: \[A_{resultant}=|2A\cos(\pi/3)|=A.\]
Why: The delayed maximum of the second oscillator is not simultaneous with the first maximum. Amplitudes therefore cannot be added as unsigned scalars.
Why not the others: (A) assumes zero phase difference. (B) uses a phase difference π/3 instead of 2π/3. (D) assumes antiphase π.
Key point: Convert a delay into phase before adding oscillations.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Two different end reflections determine pulse sign and successive return times
questions.syllabus_anchor: Waves: reflection; fixed and free boundaries; propagation time
questions.question: A short upward pulse starts at the midpoint of an ideal string, moving right. The left end is fixed and the right end is free; speed is v and total length L. Neglect losses and pulse overlap away from an end. What are the signs of the first two returned pulses observed at the midpoint and their arrival times measured from launch?
options: A) First upward at L/v; second downward at 2L/v
B) First downward at L/v; second upward at 2L/v
C) Both downward, at L/(2v) and L/v
D) Both upward, at L/v and 2L/v
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The free-end return is upward; the following fixed-end return is downward.
Given: The pulse starts halfway between two different boundary types.
Formula/Principle: Displacement reflection is noninverting at a free end and inverting at a fixed end; travel time is path length divided by speed.
Step 1: Travel midpoint→right end→midpoint has total length L. The free-end reflection retains the upward sign.
Step 2: The next leg midpoint→left end→midpoint adds another distance L. Reflection at the fixed end inverts the pulse.
Worked derivation: \[t_1=L/v,\quad t_2=2L/v,\quad (sign_1,sign_2)=(+,-).\]
Why: Boundary displacement constraints set phase independently of propagation direction. Reversing direction alone does not imply inversion.
Why not the others: (B) swaps free and fixed reflection rules. (C) uses one-way distances instead of complete return paths. (D) ignores the second fixed-end inversion.
Key point: Apply the correct boundary rule at every encounter.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Electric Charges and Fields / Electrostatic Potential
questions.sub_topic: A fixed Gaussian surface changes flux when charges exchange inside and outside positions
questions.syllabus_anchor: Electric Charges and Fields: electric flux; Gauss's law
questions.question: At stage X a closed Gaussian surface encloses +q while a separate -2q charge lies outside. At stage Y the +q charge is outside and -2q is inside; neither charge lies on the surface in either stage. The surface geometry is unchanged. What is final outward electric flux minus initial outward electric flux?
options: B) -q/ε0
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The flux change is -3q/ε0.
Given: Charge positions relative to the surface change while its area does not.
Formula/Principle: Net outward electric flux is enclosed charge divided by ε0.
Step 1: \[\Phi_X=q/\varepsilon_0,\qquad\Phi_Y=-2q/\varepsilon_0.\]
Step 2: \[\Delta\Phi=\Phi_Y-\Phi_X=-3q/\varepsilon_0.\]
Worked derivation: The same signed result follows from +q leaving and -2q entering: \(\Delta Q_{inside}=-q-2q=-3q\).
Why: External charges can change the field on parts of a surface without adding net enclosed charge. Surface area alone does not fix the flux.
Why not the others: (A) reverses final minus initial. (B) combines the two charge values without tracking which side contains them. (C) assumes unchanged geometry implies unchanged flux.
Key point: Track signed charge crossing the boundary, not only surface area.
questions.image_alt: The +q and -2q charges exchange inside and outside positions between stages X and Y.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Potentiometer null removes tested-cell loading from an emf comparison
questions.syllabus_anchor: Current Electricity: potentiometer; internal resistance
questions.question: A potentiometer with unchanged uniform potential gradient balances two cells at 60.0 cm and 90.0 cm. Their internal resistances are different, but each balance is a true null with no current drawn from the tested cell. What is E1/E2, and why are their internal resistances irrelevant to that ratio?
options: A) 3/2; because resistance is always irrelevant in any voltage measurement
B) 2/3; at null the tested cell has no internal voltage drop
C) 1; because the same potentiometer wire is used
D) 2/3; because both tested cells carry identical nonzero current
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) E1/E2=2/3; the tested-cell current vanishes at each null.
Given: Potential gradient is fixed between the two comparisons.
Formula/Principle: At balance E=kℓ because no current is drawn from the test branch.
Step 1: \[E_1/E_2=(k\cdot60)/(k\cdot90)=2/3.\]
Step 2: A test-cell internal drop is Ir; at a true null I=0 for that branch, so its internal resistance does not lower the balanced emf.
Worked derivation: \[I_1r_1=I_2r_2=0\] without requiring r1=r2.
Why: A null comparison differs from a finite-resistance voltmeter that draws current and can measure a loaded terminal voltage.
Why not the others: (A) inverts the length ratio and overgeneralises resistance irrelevance. (C) ignores different balance lengths. (D) contradicts the null condition.
Key point: Identify the branch whose current is zero.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: An inductor can return energy with unchanged current direction and reversed terminal voltage
questions.syllabus_anchor: Electromagnetic Induction: self-inductance; energy
questions.question: The ideal inductor in the diagram has current I=I0 sin(ωt) entering terminal A and leaving B. At t=3π/(4ω), which signs describe I, terminal voltage VA-VB and the rate of change of its stored energy?
options: A) I positive; voltage positive; energy increasing
B) I negative; voltage negative; energy increasing
C) I positive; voltage negative; energy decreasing
D) I positive; voltage zero; energy constant
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Current remains positive, voltage is negative and stored energy is falling.
Given: The terminal voltage uses the passive convention, with current entering A.
Formula/Principle: \(V_A-V_B=L\,dI/dt\) and \(dU/dt=LI\,dI/dt\).
Step 1: At ωt=3π/4, \[I=I_0/\sqrt2>0,\quad dI/dt=-\omega I_0/\sqrt2<0.\]
Step 2: \[V_A-V_B=-L\omega I_0/\sqrt2<0.\]
Worked derivation: \[dU/dt=-L\omega I_0^2/2<0.\]
Why: Voltage sign responds to the change of current, not to current sign alone. Here the inductor returns magnetic energy while current still flows in its original direction.
Why not the others: (A) assigns the increasing-current signs. (B) confuses negative slope with negative current. (D) uses the current maximum time instead of the stated time.
Key point: Distinguish current, current derivative and energy-flow signs.
questions.image_alt: At the marked phase current is positive on the descending part of a sine curve; current enters terminal A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Loaded transformer terminal voltage and efficiency include winding and core losses
questions.syllabus_anchor: Alternating Current: transformers; power and efficiency
questions.question: A transformer model uses the ideal induced-emf turns relation with Np/Ns=5 and primary voltage 100 V rms. Its secondary winding has resistance 1 ohm and supplies a 4 ohm resistor. Core loss is 20 W and all other losses are neglected. What are the delivered load power and efficiency?
options: A) 80 W; 80 percent
B) 64 W; 80 percent
C) 100 W; 64 percent
D) 64 W; 64 percent
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Load power is 64 W and efficiency 64 percent.
Given: Secondary induced emf is not identical to loaded terminal voltage because its winding resistance is retained.
Formula/Principle: Find secondary current through winding plus load, then include all stated losses in input power.
Step 1: \[E_s=100/5=20\ \mathrm V,\quad I_s=20/(1+4)=4\ \mathrm A.\]
Step 2: \[P_{load}=I_s^2(4)=64\ \mathrm W,\quad P_{Cu}=I_s^2(1)=16\ \mathrm W.\]
Step 3: Input power supplies load plus copper and core losses.
Worked derivation: \[\eta=\frac{64}{64+16+20}=0.64.\]
Why: The turns relation applies to the induced emf in this model, while the load voltage is reduced by the secondary winding drop. Efficiency counts core loss in addition to copper loss.
Why not the others: (A) treats induced emf as load voltage. (B) omits the core loss from input. (C) calls the input power the delivered load power.
Key point: Separate induced emf, terminal voltage and the full power budget.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Eyepiece translation changes telescope image distance and angular magnification
questions.syllabus_anchor: Ray Optics: telescope; lens formula; angular magnification
questions.question: An astronomical telescope has objective focal length 80 cm and eyepiece focal length 5 cm. It is initially normally adjusted for a distant object. The eyepiece alone is moved 1 cm toward the objective. What are the final image distance measured from the eyepiece with Cartesian signs and the magnitude of the angular magnification? Use paraxial angles and an eye close to the eyepiece.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The final image distance is -20 cm and angular magnification magnitude is 20.
Given: The objective still forms its real image 80 cm behind it; the moved eyepiece is 84 cm behind it.
Formula/Principle: Apply the eyepiece lens formula and compare the output angle with the original distant-object angle.
Step 1: Eyepiece object distance is u=-4 cm. \[1/5=1/v-1/(-4)\ \Rightarrow\ 1/v=-1/20,\quad v=-20\ \mathrm{cm}.\]
Step 2: If intermediate height is h, its virtual image height is \((v/u)h=5h\). The output angle magnitude is 5h/20=h/4.
Worked derivation: \[|M|=(h/4)/(h/80)=20.\]
Why: Moving the eyepiece changes the finite-image setting but does not move the objective's intermediate image for the same distant object.
Why not the others: (B) gives a real instead of virtual final image. (C) retains normal-adjustment magnification. (D) reports the eyepiece object distance as its image distance.
Key point: Locate the unchanged intermediate image before applying the moved eyepiece.

questions.sub_topic: Coincident diffraction zeros remove interference orders at the central-envelope boundary
questions.syllabus_anchor: Wave Optics: interference; single-slit diffraction
questions.question: Two identical slits of width a have centre separation d=3a. Use interference maxima d sinθ=mλ and single-slit diffraction minima a sinθ=nλ, with nonzero integer n. Which is the first missing noncentral interference order, and how many bright interference maxima remain strictly inside the central diffraction envelope?
options: A) Second order; three maxima
B) Third order; seven maxima
C) Third order; five maxima
D) Sixth order; five maxima
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The third order is first missing and five interference maxima lie inside the central envelope.
Given: The diffraction envelope's first minima occur at |a sinθ|=λ.
Formula/Principle: A nominal interference maximum disappears when it coincides with a diffraction minimum.
Step 1: Equating the two angular conditions gives \[m\lambda/d=n\lambda/a\ \Rightarrow\ m=3n.\] The first nonzero missing order is |m|=3.
Step 2: Strictly within the central envelope, \(|m|<d/a=3\).
Worked derivation: Allowed bright orders are \[-2,-1,0,1,2,\] giving five.
Why: The envelope boundary orders ±3 cannot be counted as bright because the individual-slit amplitude vanishes there.
Why not the others: (A) confuses d/a with another order relation. (B) counts the extinguished boundary maxima. (D) skips the first coincident diffraction zero.
Key point: Apply the interference condition together with the finite-slit envelope.

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.sub_topic: A fixed total energy makes wavelength-product minimisation different from equal-momentum allocation
questions.syllabus_anchor: Dual Nature: matter wavelengths; kinetic energy; constrained quadratic maximum
questions.question: Two nonrelativistic particles have masses m and 4m and freely adjustable positive kinetic energies KA,KB with fixed sum K. Which division minimises the product of their de Broglie wavelengths, and what is λA/λB at that minimum?
options: A) KA=4K/5, KB=K/5; ratio 1
B) KA=KB=K/2; ratio 2
C) KA=KB=K/2; ratio 1
D) KA=K/5, KB=4K/5; ratio 4
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Equal kinetic energies minimise the wavelength product, and λA/λB=2 there.
Given: Total kinetic energy K is fixed and both shares are positive.
Formula/Principle: \(\lambda=h/\sqrt{2mK_i}\); minimising the product is equivalent to maximising KA KB.
Step 1: \[\lambda_A\lambda_B=\frac{h^2}{4m\sqrt{K_AK_B}}.\]
Step 2: Since \[K_AK_B=K_A(K-K_A)=K^2/4-(K_A-K/2)^2,\] it is largest at equal shares.
Step 3: Equal energies give momentum ratio pB/pA=√(4m/m)=2.
Worked derivation: \[\lambda_A/\lambda_B=p_B/p_A=2,\quad(\lambda_A\lambda_B)_{min}=h^2/(2mK).\]
Why: Equal momentum would produce equal wavelengths but would not maximise the kinetic-energy product. These are different constraints.
Why not the others: (A) gives equal momenta rather than the required minimum. (C) assumes equal energy means equal momentum for unequal masses. (D) does not maximise the energy product.
Key point: Optimise under the stated fixed sum before imposing a wavelength comparison.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Donor ionisation changes majority carriers while fixed-ion compensation preserves bulk neutrality
questions.syllabus_anchor: Semiconductor Electronics: extrinsic semiconductor; donors; charge neutrality
questions.question: A silicon crystal is doped with dilute pentavalent donors. In a uniform bulk region each donor is ionised once, no external charge has been added, and electron concentration greatly exceeds hole concentration. Which description preserves both carrier identity and bulk charge accounting?
options: A) The bulk must be negatively charged because mobile electrons are majority carriers
B) Positive donor ions move through the crystal as its main current carriers
C) The ionised donors are negatively charged and holes are the majority carriers
D) Electrons are majority mobile carriers; positive fixed donor ions balance their excess charge approximately in the neutral bulk
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Mobile majority electrons coexist with compensating positive ionised donors.
Given: The donor supplies an extra electron but the initially neutral material has not received net external charge.
Formula/Principle: Track the donor's charge after ionisation and distinguish mobile carriers from fixed lattice ions.
Step 1: A donated electron contributes negative mobile charge, while its donor becomes a positively charged fixed centre.
Step 2: Bulk neutrality requires \[n\simeq N_D^+\] when the small hole concentration is neglected; more exactly \(n=p+N_D^+\) in the stated donor-only bulk.
Worked derivation: The charge density is \[\rho=e(p+N_D^+-n)\simeq0.\]
Why: N-type means electron-majority conduction, not a macroscopic negative charge. Ionisation redistributes existing charge between mobile and lattice-associated forms.
Why not the others: (A) omits compensating donor charge. (B) confuses fixed ions with mobile electronic carriers. (C) reverses both donor-ion sign and majority-carrier type.
Key point: Majority carrier type and net bulk charge are distinct concepts.
